Cheating or not cheating? Rethinking AI-giarism and academic integrity through secondary students’ ethical reasoning
abstract: The increasing use of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in education has complicated traditional understandings of academic integrity, particularly in relation to student cheating. This qualitative study explores how secondary school students’ reason about the ethicality of using AI in homework, moving beyond binary interpretations of cheating. Drawing on Waltzer and Dahl’s moral-developmental framework, the study analysed open-ended responses from 133 students aged 14–16 who participated in an online AI literacy programme in Hong Kong. The findings show that students engage in conditional and context-sensitive ethical reasoning, considering factors such as purpose of use, learning impact, intent, and fairness. Rather than viewing AI use as inherently unethical, students positioned themselves as active moral agents who interpret ambiguous rules, evaluate acceptability, and make situational decisions about action. The study challenges fixed notions of AI-giarism and academic misconduct, highlighting the need to rethink academic integrity, assessment design, and AI literacy education in ways that foreground ethical reasoning, transparency, and student agency.

title: Color me confounded: A critical analysis of media comparisons on ChatGPT in education
abstract: Research on the use of artificial intelligence in education is rapidly accumulating. In the ChatGPT literature, two recent meta-analyses were published (Deng et al., 2025 and Wang & Fan, 2025) that examined media comparisons between ChatGPT and more traditional forms of instruction; both reviews found ChatGPT to improve learning. However, as researchers have found in media comparisons studies (e.g., Clark, 1983; Lawson et al., 2024), instructional methods are often not controlled between conditions, making it difficult to attribute any learning differences to affordances of the medium itself. Therefore, the purpose of our critical review was to examine those media comparisons studies included in Deng et al. (2025) and Wang and Fan (2025) to understand whether the ChatGPT and control conditions were comparable on their instructional features (i.e., matched on instructional methods, practice with the dependent measure, and time spent learning the content). Results indicated a lack of control in the ChatGPT studies that were reviewed, with many studies conflating the use of ChatGPT with other instructional features. Further, across the various direct learning outcomes, studies often did not include enough information to determine the comparability of conditions. For the most common learning outcome (i.e., ChatGPT > Control), comparisons often involved a confound between conditions as well as missing information about instructional features. Therefore, the benefits of ChatGPT must be interpreted with caution at the present time, and more research is needed to determine how, for whom, and under what pedagogical conditions ChatGPT can improve learning.

title: Unlocking the potential of resources: An examination of sharing and uptake signs in educational online communities
abstract: Educational resources like teaching materials, worksheets, and other instructional content are an essential source of teachers’ classroom practice. Prior research suggests that teachers use social media to acquire and share such resources, yet little is known about whether social media interaction indicate teacher’s resource-uptake for classroom practice. Drawing on an affinity-space perspective, this study examines how teacher-oriented educational resources are shared and responded to in four German teacher-oriented hashtag communities on Twitter (now X ). The dataset comprises 2,064,799 tweets from 116,967 users and covers activity from 2008 to 2021. Using qualitative and quantitative analyses, we investigate the distribution of resource-containing tweets, the sentiment of replies, and replies containing language that indicates intended or reported classroom use. Results show that links and media are not shared equally across community types and that replies to tweets containing potential educational resources are generally positive in tone. Across communities, approximately 2.2% to 3.1% of replies to resource-containing tweets contain language suggesting intended or reported classroom use. In addition, higher user centrality and, in some communities, teacher status are associated with more positive responses to resource-containing tweets and a greater likelihood of uptake-indicating replies. The study contributes to research on teachers’ informal professional learning by showing how teacher-oriented social media spaces may support the circulation of resources and generate limited signals of possible classroom uptake.

title: Searching for predictors of presence, academic achievement and satisfaction in online adult education
abstract: Little attention has been paid to adults pursuing online education at the upper secondary level. The aim of this article is to identify and describe predictors of presence, academic achievement, and satisfaction in online upper secondary education for adults. The study is grounded in the Community of Inquiry (CoI) framework, which is based on three types of presence: teaching presence (TP), social presence (SP), and cognitive presence (CP). A survey was administered to adults who had completed, or were close to completing, an online upper secondary-level course in Sweden, yielding 672 responses. An exploratory factor analysis showed that items from the CP and TP constructs related to peer interaction and teacher guidance loaded onto the SP construct instead. Accordingly, the factors were labeled as individual TP (iTP), extended SP (eSP), and individual CP (iCP) to describe how the CoI framework is manifested in this context, characterized by substantial individual study and varying opportunities for social interaction. Multiple regression models explained a substantial proportion of the variance in iTP (adjusted R 2 = .58), eSP (adjusted R 2 = .68), and satisfaction (adjusted R 2 = .53), a more moderate proportion in iCP (adjusted R 2 = .36) and only a small proportion for academic achievement (adjusted R 2 = .13). Academic achievement was primarily associated with iCP ( β = .38), whereas student satisfaction was primarily associated with iTP ( β = .58). Key predictors included course introductions related to studying and technology, tutoring, synchronous online teaching, and collaborative course design.

title: Fostering digital confidence and collaborative creativity in pre-service teachers: Evaluating change through a convergence, divergence, and synergy lens
Operationalizing cognitive apprenticeship through generative AI pedagogical agents: Proactive and contextualized guidance in simulation-based learning
A community of inquiry perspective on human–AI co-facilitation within micro-blended learning
abstract: This study explores the distribution of teaching, social, and cognitive presences across human teachers and artificial intelligence (AI) systems in micro-blended learning environments for K–12 mathematics education, framed by the Community of Inquiry (CoI) framework. Utilizing a semester-long experimental design in high school Algebra classes, the instruction alternated between teacher-led in-person sessions and AI-facilitated online learning using MathPal, a conversational AI agent. The findings reveal a complementary relationship between teacher-led instruction and AI contributions, where teachers provided foundational conceptual scaffolds, affective support, and responsive guidance, while MathPal extended learning through step-by-step individualized scaffolding, adaptive feedback, and socio-emotional reinforcement. Sequential interaction analysis and hierarchical regression indicate that MathPal strengthened instructional continuity and engagement, while teacher-driven scaffolds remained the strongest predictor of mathematical reasoning outcomes. Based on these findings, this study introduces the Distributed Community of Inquiry framework, expanding CoI theory to address emerging dynamics in teacher-AI collaboration. Practical implications include optimizing modality alignment, embedding adaptive relational features into AI systems, and incorporating scalable learning designs that support equitable access to instructional support. This research contributes insights into the synergy between human and AI facilitators within micro-blended learning environments and highlights areas for future research, including broader validation across disciplines and AI platforms.

title: Mapping teacher education strategies to develop digital competence targets: A cross-framework analysis
abstract: Rapid technological developments are reshaping expectations regarding teachers' digital competence targets, challenging teacher education programmes to design learning experiences that systematically support its development. This study examines how digital competence targets and teacher education strategies intersect within authentic teacher education practices. Drawing on the European DigCompEdu Framework and the second Synthesis of Qualitative Data (SQD2) model, the study analyses 33 documented teacher education practices implemented across five universities. Using quantitative content analysis combined with co-occurrence and network analysis, the study maps (1) the digital competence targets addressed, (2) the SQD2 strategies enacted, and (3) the patterns of association between digital competence targets and teacher education strategies. The findings indicate that pedagogically oriented competence targets related to teaching practice and professional reflection, particularly Reflective practice (1.3) and Teaching (3.1), are most prominently represented across the documented practices. These digital competence targets consistently co-occur with a coherent set of teacher education strategies, including hands-on experience, pedagogical reasoning, and teacher identity development. In contrast, digital competence targets related to technical problem-solving, digital safety, and technological infrastructure appear only marginally or remain largely implicit within the analysed practices. The findings further underscore the importance of curriculum coherence and pedagogical orchestration in supporting the development of pre-service teachers’ digital competence targets.

title: Preparing undergraduate education majors to make and use accessible digital instructional materials
Analysing student engagement in breakout rooms in an online language course
abstract: As the popularity of online courses in higher education keeps increasing, the importance of student engagement gets highlighted. In an online learning environment, peer interaction gets emphasised when students work in small groups in breakout rooms. In this case study, qualitative content analysis and discourse analysis were used to analyse breakout room recordings (458 minutes in total) of two small groups in a 14-week synchronous online language course. The study focused on how engagement at small group level seems to emerge from the group’s interaction, which is a primordial site for language learning, and what kind of collaborative engagement practices seem to support it. The findings suggest that affective, behavioural, and cognitive engagement often co-occur and that they may either support or hinder each other. Also, the group members may be engaged in diverse ways at the same time. Three collaborative engagement practices were identified: participation in group discussions, making and negotiating proposals, and collaborative writing. Participation in group discussions highlighted the importance of both verbal and nonverbal communication and the importance of equity in participation. When making proposals, the role of tentativeness was emphasised as that seemed to open space for interaction in the small group. Finally, collaborative writing was found to engage students specifically from the language learning perspective. The findings suggest that small group interaction and collaboration play a key role in group level engagement. It is suggested that small group level should be taken into consideration when operationalising the concept of engagement in online learning environments.

title: Editorial Board
Educational prompt engineering self-efficacy scale (Ed-PESS): Development and psychometric validation
abstract: Abstract Pre-service teachers' confidence in designing pedagogically purposeful prompts for generative AI tools remains an underexamined construct in teacher education. This study developed and validated the Educational Prompt Engineering Self-Efficacy Scale for Pre-service Teachers (Ed-PESS) to address the absence of a psychometrically sound instrument measuring this domain. Scale development followed Boateng et al.'s three-phase framework, grounded in a systematic literature review and expert review procedures. Two independent samples of pre-service teachers were recruited: an exploratory factor analysis (EFA) sample (n = 300) and a confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) sample (n = 305). EFA using principal axis factoring with Promax rotation produced a four-factor structure explaining 64.60% of total variance. CFA with Yuan-Bentler robust correction confirmed acceptable model fit. The final 26-item scale comprises four dimensions: Basic Prompt Engineering, Pedagogical Prompt Engineering, Ethical Prompting Practice, and Continuous Professional Development. Internal consistency was high across all subscales. The Ed-PESS provides a valid, reliable instrument for assessing prompt engineering self-efficacy in pre-service teacher education. It supports formative curriculum evaluation and targeted intervention design.

LLM-derived metrics in second language writing assessment: an explainable AI approach
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in educational technology for automated writing assessment, yet most applications rely on prompt-based scoring and feedback generation, which often lack transparency, reproducibility, and interpretability. This study investigates whether model-internal LLM representations can provide interpretable and reproducible metrics for second language (L2) writing assessment. We derived surprisal and perplexity from next-token prediction to quantify linguistic predictability and embedding-based similarity to measure semantic coherence across sentences. These metrics were computed at the token, sentence, and discourse levels using three pretrained Chinese language models and evaluated on 1,196 essays written by Chinese L2 learners across four proficiency levels. Their relationships with 11 established linguistic measures of fluency, lexical sophistication, phraseological complexity, and syntactic complexity were also examined. Results showed that surprisal and perplexity generally decreased with proficiency for the two Traditional Chinese-focused models, indicating greater linguistic predictability in more proficient writing, whereas the multilingual model showed weaker sensitivity. Embedding-based similarity increased with proficiency, reflecting stronger semantic coherence. Combining LLM-derived metrics with classical linguistic features improved proficiency classification and prediction beyond either feature set alone. Correlation and qualitative analyses further demonstrated that the proposed metrics capture complementary aspects of writing while revealing conditions under which their interpretations become less reliable. These findings demonstrate the value of interpretable, model-derived metrics for transparent, reproducible, and scalable AI-supported L2 writing assessment, particularly for underrepresented learner populations and lower-resource languages.

title: Designing effective feedback in video lectures using GenAI: The roles of feedback type and learner agency in error detection
Artificial intelligence in educational leadership: A PRISMA-Guided bibliometric review and agenda for future research
abstract: Research on artificial intelligence (AI) in educational leadership is expanding rapidly but remains fragmented. This study synthesises the field through a PRISMA-guided bibliometric analysis of 219 peer-reviewed articles from Web of Science and Scopus and develops an agenda for future research. Using VOSviewer, we mapped the field's evolution, prolific authors and journals, and keyword co-occurrence networks, identifying five thematic domains: foundational technologies, student- and teacher-facing applications, data-driven analytics, systems integration, and algorithmic decision support. Results reveal sharp post-2020 growth, disciplinary dispersion, and concentration in higher education and a small number of regions. Building on these patterns, the study proposes a future research agenda focused on geographic scope, educational level, ethical governance, longitudinal implementation, generative AI governance, and theoretical integration. The study advances the literature by consolidating fragmented insights into a taxonomy that reframes AI as an evolving governance ecosystem and by clarifying the key gaps that should shape future research on responsible AI adoption in educational leadership.

title: The experience of using AI-generated social stories as a behavioral intervention tool for children
abstract: As artificial intelligence becomes increasingly integrated into educational and therapeutic settings, understanding professional user experience with AI-generated interventions is crucial for successful implementation. This study examines how education and therapy professionals experience using social stories created by AI versus human experts for children with special needs. Using a 2×2 experimental design, 227 female professionals in Israel evaluated social stories designed to either promote positive behaviors or reduce challenging behaviors, with authorship randomly attributed to either AI (Claude) or a human speech therapist. All stories were actually AI-generated, allowing isolated examination of authorship perception effects. Results revealed no main effects for creator type or story purpose, but significant Creator × Purpose interactions emerged for understanding, feasibility, and overall user experience. AI-generated stories were rated more favorably for behavior promotion interventions, while human-authored stories were preferred for behavior reduction interventions. User experience ratings remained stable across conditions, suggesting fundamental legitimacy of both approaches. Professionals working with younger children reported significantly better user experience compared to those working with adolescents, while professional experience and field showed no influence on user experience evaluations. These findings challenge assumptions about AI resistance in sensitive professional contexts and reveal the importance of strategic alignment between intervention purpose and perceived creator expertise. The results provide evidence-based guidance for integrating AI tools in special education, suggesting that AI may be particularly valuable for promoting positive behaviors while human expertise remains preferred for addressing complex behavioral challenges.

Fifty years of topic development, thematic combination, and AI's evolving reach in Computers & Education
abstract: Across the first fifty years of Computers & Education , successive technologies entered an expanding educational agenda centered on teaching, learning, learner regulation, assessment, participation, access, and institutional conditions. This study examined how that agenda developed from 1976 through partial 2026. We assembled 5,739 records, retained 5,388 eligible articles and reviews, and modeled 5,387 records using titles and available abstracts. An eighteen-topic structural topic model traced topic prevalence across five historical periods. Ordered primary–secondary topic combinations examined changing within-article co-occurrence patterns, while a validated dictionary and continuous piecewise binomial logistic models traced artificial intelligence (AI) prevalence and topical integration. Early volumes concentrated on computer-assisted learning, educational software, and intelligent systems; later research gave greater attention to teacher integration, collaboration, learning analytics, learner regulation, digital literacy, and feedback. Within-article topic combinations diversified substantially across the archive. The share represented by the ten most frequent topic combinations fell from 74.4% in 1976–1989 to 16.5% in 2010–2019, indicating substantial diversification. The human-validated AI corpus contained 390 records (7.2%) and extended across 17 of the 18 topics. Annual modeling identified marked acceleration in AI-related publication prevalence after 2018, as research on generative models expanded alongside established AI traditions. This acceleration reflects growing research attention, not demonstrated educational effectiveness. Across fifty years, the journal broadened how it addressed enduring educational questions. These findings call for evaluating AI within its educational configuration, with attention to human agency, theoretical and disciplinary grounding, and evidence of effectiveness in authentic learning settings.

title: Mapping fifty years of technology-enhanced science and mathematics education in Computers & Education: Trends and connections with technologies, functions, and theories
abstract: This study reviewed 50 years of research on technology-enhanced science and mathematics education published in Computers & Education (1976–2026). Following PRISMA 2020 framework, 519 empirical studies were retained. BERTopic-based topic modeling was applied to derive the thematic structure of the corpus, and each article was coded for education level, theoretical framework, primary technology, and technology function. Seventeen topics were identified, including ten science-related, four mathematics-related, and three domain-general ones. Topic membership was more strongly associated with primary technology and technology function than with education level and theoretical framework. Game-based learning split into separate science and mathematics topics, and a mathematics-centered AI/agent topic emerged, while AI-related science studies were found to be assigned to existing topics such as argumentation, collaborative learning, and inquiry. VR was a distinct technological topic and served several instructional functions. Besides, research within this corpus shifted from computer-centered instructional agendas toward a more diverse space encompassing learning analytics, games, mobile and immersive environments, eye tracking, and AI, with integrated STEM and eye-tracking topics emerging in this corpus around the mid-2010s. Science-related work differentiated around disciplinary practices, whereas mathematics-related work clustered around forms of instructional support rather than mathematical subdomains. Future work can extend the BERTopic framework to a broader set of journals to fully understand the overall trends, or apply BERTopic method separately to publications within fixed intervals to examine how research topics evolve over time.

title: Topic landscapes and cross-period semantic connections in Computers & Education
abstract: For the 50th anniversary of Computers & Education, this study describes the topic landscape and cross-period semantic connections among 5,226 articles published from 1980 to 18 June 2026. Independently fitted BERTopic models for 1980–2003, 2004–2013, 2014–2019, and 2020–2026 identified 11, 15, 18, and 9 non-noise topics, respectively. We examine publication shares, exploratory annual trends, semantic similarity networks between adjacent periods, and within-period associations with a predefined artificial intelligence (AI) vocabulary. The retained semantic similarity networks include 22, 30, and 36 topic-level connections across the three adjacent-period comparisons. These networks consist mainly of one-to-many and many-to-many components rather than one-to-one correspondences. The 2014–2019 and 2020–2026 comparison contains one many-to-many component without unlinked nodes, whereas the earlier comparisons contain multiple connected components and several unlinked target topics. In 2020–2026, online learning and teacher competence have the largest publication shares, while generative AI shows the strongest association with the selected AI vocabulary. These analyses provide descriptive evidence on topic prevalence, annual trends, cross-period semantic similarity, and AI vocabulary association. The results should be interpreted within the scope of corpus coverage, modeling decisions, period definitions, and vocabulary selection, and do not imply causal relations or historical processes beyond the observed semantic patterns.

title: Agency and adaptation in human–technology configurations: A fifty-year analysis of Computers & Education
abstract: Educational-technology histories are often organized around successive tools, obscuring how action, decision-making, regulation, and adaptive work are distributed among human and technological actors. Drawing on 5,387 papers published in Computers & Education over fifty years, this study examines how Agency and Adaptation were configured and redistributed across learners, educators, communities, institutions, and technological systems. A purposive calibration corpus of 48 papers containing explicit Agency discourse was coded using eight Agency–Adaptation indicators comprising 63 category levels. Applying an 18-topic structural topic model as semantic infrastructure, category probabilities were projected to the full corpus through a theta-weighted linear mixture with Dirichlet-style smoothing. Clustering identified five recurring profiles: system agency–programmed adaptation, teacher/institutional agency–orchestrated adaptation, community agency–collaborative adaptation, learner agency–customization-based adaptation, and system agency–algorithmic adaptation. Although period-level distributions of prominent individual categories changed modestly, the relative prevalence of the five profiles shifted substantially, while all five continued to coexist. Historical change involved the recombination and redistribution of human and technological responsibilities, not a uniform movement from human to technological control. An exploratory analysis identified 71 GenAI-explicit papers published during 2023–2026. These papers appeared across all five profiles during this period but were concentrated in system-programmed configurations and were comparatively uncommon in learner-customization configurations relative to contemporaneous non-GenAI papers. The findings show that technological innovation alone does not specify where agency resides or how adaptation is enacted. Understanding educational-technology development requires examining complete arrangements of actors, authority, regulation, and adaptive work, including whether increasingly adaptive systems preserve meaningful opportunities for human direction, evaluation, and recalibration.

title: How we study what we study: A methodological review of 50 years of educational technology research
abstract: Research in educational technology has been extensively mapped in terms of what has been studied, but far less attention has been paid to how it has been studied. This paper reports a methodological review of fifty years of research in Computers & Education, covering a corpus of 5,516 articles published between 1976 and 2026, with the principal findings based on the post-1996 full-text corpus. Using an AI-assisted analysis, applied to full texts and abstracts, we traced the evolution of research paradigms, approaches, and methods across the journal's full publication history. The principal findings are based on the post-1996 full-text corpus. Pre-1996, full-text machine-readable files were not available for analysis. Analysis of pre-1996 abstracts was possible and are included to provide context for trends observed post-1996. The findings show that quantitative approaches and questionnaire-based data collection have constituted the field's sustained methodological centre of gravity. Within this dominant pattern, two shifts stand out: 1) the rise of systematic reviews as a recognised approach, and 2) a computational turn. The range of methods used in research has grown steadily, suggesting a gradual broadening of the field's repertoire. These patterns are only visible across multiple decades. Findings reveal that quantitative dominance is not a recent development but a persistent structural feature, and that the computational surge is better understood as a second wave following a peak in the mid-2000s. These findings have implications for what kinds of knowledge educational technology research is equipped to produce. The study argues that understanding a field's methodological history is a prerequisite for extending it.

title: Online learner engagement and academic support in the age of generative AI
Technology-enhanced second language learning in Computers & Education: A 50-year review of outcomes, technical affordances, theoretical frameworks, and their connections
abstract: Technology-enhanced second language learning (TEL2L) has been rapidly expanding as a prominent research strand over the past five decades, yet systematic reviews focusing specifically on how theoretical frameworks connect technical affordances to L2 outcomes remain scarce. To address this gap, this study presents a systematic review of TEL2L research published in Computers & Education over five decades, focusing on three interconnected dimensions: L2 learning outcomes, technical affordances, and theoretical frameworks. One hundred and twenty-two empirical articles were included after screening based on predefined criteria and analysed following the PRISMA framework, using a hybrid deductive-inductive thematic analysis and a framework and narrative synthesis. The findings revealed both an increasingly broad distribution of L2 outcome priorities and a broadly positive pattern of reported outcomes in TEL2L, with vocabulary and speaking recording the highest proportions of positive outcome reports. Twenty-four technical affordances were organised into seven functional categories, and 57 theoretical frameworks were identified across six categories, with Constructivism, Sociocultural Theory, Cognitive Load Theory, the Cognitive Theory of Multimedia Learning, and Krashen’s Monitor Model most frequently applied. Drawing on these findings, synthesised, theory-associated models of TEL2L activity were proposed, characterising the outcome and technical affordance profiles of each predominant framework. These models are intended to serve as descriptive heuristic resources for theory-driven instructional design and the empirical inquiry of emerging educational technologies.

title: Artificial intelligence in higher education (2019–2026): A systematic review of applications and an evidence-derived multi-axial taxonomy
abstract: Generative and agentic artificial intelligence (AI) have expanded AI functions in higher education, challenging taxonomies developed before the generative-AI wave. Following PRISMA 2020, we reviewed 228 peer-reviewed journal publications from January 2019 to March 2026. The publication was the coding unit; codes represented the dominant educational AI use foregrounded in each publication. Inter-coder agreement was near-perfect for the Axis 1 coding scheme (Cohen’s κ = 0.98) and substantial overall for the observed interpretive distinctions (κ = 0.69–0.78). Full-corpus mapping placed 164 of 228 publications (71.9%) outside the four original Zawacki-Richter et al. (2019) categories, but this included transversal ethics/governance and adjacent scholarly-practice literature. The functional-adequacy test therefore used the 154 publications with a classifiable application-focused function: 64 (41.6%) fit the original four categories, whereas 90 (58.4%) required one of three additional domains—AI-enabled student support, content creation and instructional design, or institutional analytics and management. This result was essentially unchanged after removing the 2023 cohort (39/67, 58.2%), and all three added domains persisted in the held-out 2026 search block. Within functional categories, applications also differed in agency, epistemic position, and pedagogy. For agency, the corpus supports an observed assistive–augmentative–delegative gradient; the autonomous endpoint is retained as a prospective theoretical category rather than an empirically validated level. Pedagogical paradigm was less stable and remains the most provisional interpretive axis. We propose a configurational four-axis framework with ethics and equity as a transversal layer, intended to support decisions about oversight, verification, pedagogical alignment and governance rather than to predict educational outcomes.

title: Fifty years of Computers & Education: Continuities, transformations, and diversification in educational technology research
